    Huron · Implementation atlas

    Security: Authentication

    Four credential paths, one frozen principal: Security owns resolution, login, persisted sessions, identity administration and self-access; the API owns browser transport.

    Security owner4 credential paths10 UML viewsOffline-ready

    Implementation snapshot: 16 September 2026, working tree based on e71e685. The editable Markdown source contains all Mermaid diagrams and responsibility notes.

    Authentication turns whatever credential a request carries into one frozen Principal, and owns login through persisted session issuance. Four credential paths exist: an hk_ API key, an hs_ session cookie, an OIDC bearer token, and, in development only, asserted headers. Authentication and RBAC are views of core.security, which owns credential formats, resolvers, persistence ports, errors, authentication workflows and authorized identity administration. PostgreSQL and memory adapters live in core.metastore. The API owns credential extraction, cookies, CSRF, redirects, serialization and resource lifetime; Security imports no web framework or adapters.

    This is one class model presented in focused views. It includes every class and protocol retained from the authentication model, the module-level functions that mint and parse credentials, Security's identity and authentication workflows, the four PostgreSQL and four memory credential adapters, and application collaboration: the request credential dependency, the cookie specifications, the /auth routes, and the runtime bundle. Repeated boxes denote the same class. The RBAC engine, AccessPolicy, and the route guards belong to the RBAC atlas; they appear here only where a Principal is handed to them. Methods show the public operations and important types, with long parameter lists abbreviated. This is a Python class diagram, not a database ER diagram or an exhaustive signature reference.

    Currency matters: the authentication design describes the intended request model and lists its known gaps. This atlas follows the inspected source, including uncommitted changes, and records below where the code carries a field or a declaration that no consumer reads. A protocol, record field, or error name alone does not prove that a behavior is enforced.

    Reading the diagrams

    • A --> B: association/reference, including a held store or dependency.
    • A ..> B: uses, creates, or returns B; the label states which.
    • A *-- B: A contains B as part of its object structure.
    • A --|> B: actual Python inheritance.
    • A ..|> B: structural conformance to a Python protocol, not inheritance.
    • <<Protocol>>, <<Frozen>>, <<Module>>, <<Neighbor>>, <<External>>, and <<Function>> identify roles. A <<Module>> box lists module-level functions and constants that have no class of their own; a <<Function>> box is a single FastAPI dependency or helper function shown for wiring.
    • Frozen dataclasses prevent field reassignment; credential mechanism records are frozen with slots=True, and stores that change a record store a copy.
    • Store protocols are owned by Security; its resolvers and workflows perform the reads and writes. Metastore conformance is structural, not declared inheritance.
    • Public workflow imports use core.security; _impl links locate implementations, not supported imports. Migration-wide verification remains pending.

    1. Authentication at a glance

    CredentialAuthentication.resolve takes a transport-extracted bearer_token: None means absent; a present token wins outright, including an empty string that cannot authenticate. Only an absent bearer permits session resolution and then the explicitly wired development fallback. The API owns raw header parsing: authorization.removeprefix("Bearer ").strip() for a nonempty header, otherwise None. Thus missing or actually empty headers permit fallback, while whitespace or Bearer headers produce a present empty token and are refused. Every successful branch returns the same Principal; authorization never sees the credential.

    Responsibility Owner Important contract
    Name the authenticated subject Principal Frozen snapshot taken at resolution: subject, groups, credential restrictions, method, and kind (user or service_account).
    Resolve an API key ApiKeyResolver with ApiKeyStore Parse hk_{key_id}_{secret}; hash and compare even on a miss; report revocation before expiry, both only after the secret matched.
    Resolve a session SessionResolver with SessionStore Parse hs_{session_id}_{secret}; same dummy-digest comparison; revoked before expired; slide the idle deadline at most once per TOUCH_INTERVAL, never past the absolute deadline.
    Resolve a bearer JWT OidcResolver with JwksVerifier Signature, issuer, audience, expiry and required claims are the verifier's; the resolver only maps the subject and groups claims. No store is consulted.
    Browser login OidcAuthentication, PasswordAuthentication Signed state/nonce/PKCE and identity provisioning, or bounded off-loop password verification with optional rehash; both persist sessions. Routes issue cookies.
    Provision and revoke identities IdentityService user.manage at SYSTEM for users; service_account.manage at the organization for service-account keys. Password reset and disable revoke every session and key the subject holds.
    Persist credentials Metastore adapters One table per store protocol; secrets stored only as SHA-256 or argon2 hashes; subject uniqueness and kind guards are database constraints translated to domain errors.
    Fail uniformly AuthError hierarchy Every resolver raises an AuthError whose code becomes the 401 problem code; provisioning conflicts are separate DomainError classes.

    2. Principal, resolvers, and the request credential

    Sources: principal.py, ApiKeyResolver, SessionResolver, oidc.py, dev.py, credential workflow, credentials.py.

    • Principal.scopes and Principal.project_id are populated only by ApiKeyResolver from the key's minting restrictions. No module outside credential resolution reads either field: authorization projects the principal down to subject, groups and kind before consulting bindings, so an API key's declared scope and project restriction are recorded, not enforced.
    • OidcResolver and DevHeaderResolver consult no store. A bearer JWT for a principal that has since been disabled still resolves for the token's lifetime; disabling revokes sessions and API keys, which are the only credentials the service itself issued.
    • SessionResolver.resolve() returns the principal and the record as it stands after this request; current_session exposes that record to the routes.
    • Both resolver constructors accept an optional Foundation Clock; omitted clocks use UTC wall time. An explicit resolve(..., now=...) overrides the clock. Otherwise time is sampled after awaited lookup and matching-secret verification, not at workflow entry. API-key revocation is checked before this sample; session time is sampled before its revocation check. Both report revocation before expiry. Session deadline checks, touch throttling and idle-extension arithmetic share that same post-lookup instant. CredentialAuthentication injects the clock rather than passing an early timestamp; rejected credentials cause no last-used/session touch.
    • API-key last-used bookkeeping in CredentialAuthentication is best-effort: a failure is logged and never fails the request. _enforce_csrf applies only in the cookie branch and only to methods other than GET, HEAD and OPTIONS.
    • DevHeaderResolver raises ValueError from its constructor for any environment except development; application wiring constructs it with that literal, and ApiSettings separately refuses dev-headers outside development.

    3. API keys: minting, storage, and revocation

    Sources: apikeys.py, authentication errors, Security ports, PostgreSQL API keys, memory API keys.

    ApiKeyStore is deliberately a single read; the write path is ApiKeyWriter, declared in core/security/ports.py as a protocol that extends it. Both stores satisfy the writer structurally. create_api_key() refuses a TTL that is not positive or exceeds 400 days, defaults scopes to {"read"}, and returns the only copy of the secret alongside a record that holds its SHA-256. The memory store keeps no last_used_at; its touched list exists for tests. The Postgres store translates a foreign-key violation on project_id into ResourceNotFound, and its get() returns revoked and expired rows unchanged so the resolver can report them distinctly.

    4. Sessions, cookies, and CSRF

    Sources: sessions.py, cookies.py, credentials.py, PostgreSQL sessions, memory sessions.

    Rule Where it lives
    Idle deadline IDLE_TTL (12 h) after last activity; absolute deadline ABSOLUTE_TTL (7 d) after login. create_session() sets both; SessionResolver refuses when either has passed.
    The idle deadline is persisted at most once per TOUCH_INTERVAL (5 min) and is capped at the absolute deadline. SessionResolver.resolve() uses one instant sampled after lookup and secret verification (or explicit now); the sessions table CHECK backstops the cap.
    Groups are a login-time snapshot; they refresh at the next login, not mid-session. SessionRecord.groups, copied into every resolved Principal.
    A cookie-authenticated state change must echo csrf_token in X-Huron-CSRF; bearer callers and safe methods are exempt. _enforce_csrf in the request dependency; the token is returned by login and GET /auth/session.
    Cookies are HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, and Secure outside development. The session cookie's name is configurable; the login-flow cookie is fixed to huron_login under /auth. CookieSpec with session_cookie() and login_flow_cookie().
    Revocation is a row update visible on the next request. Logout revokes by id; password reset and disable revoke by subject. SessionStore.revoke() and revoke_all_for().

    A fresh login does not revoke the session the browser previously held; only logout, an administrative password reset, or a disable ends an earlier session before its own deadlines. Password login carries no session cookie and therefore no CSRF check of its own; the design document records both as known gaps and the code matches that description.

    5. OIDC: verifier, client, and the pending-login flow

    Sources: oidc.py, OIDC workflow, OIDC runtime wiring, settings.py, app.py, routes/auth/endpoints/oidc.py.

    Two paths read one provider. The bearer path is JwksVerifier (RS256/ES256 only; exp, iat, sub required; keys cached for five minutes) feeding OidcResolver. The browser path is OidcClient.discover() at startup, then authorization_url() with a fresh LoginFlow on /auth/oidc/start, and exchange_code() on the callback, which verifies the ID token with the client's own verifier and checks the nonce. LoginFlow travels in an HMAC-signed, not encrypted, cookie under login_flow_secret; decode() verifies the signature before parsing, refuses flows older than max_age or stamped in the future, and __post_init__ refuses a non-local return_to. OidcAuthentication.finish compares the callback state in constant time.

    Application wiring passes flow_max_age=login_flow_cookie(settings).max_age into OidcAuthentication, so the signed-flow validator uses the same lifetime as the issued pending-login cookie. The deployed lifetime is 600 seconds; Security receives that plain value and does not interpret cookies or deployment settings.

    When create_app receives an injected oidc_verify callable, only OidcResolver is built and the OIDC routes answer OidcNotConfigured. OidcProviderConfig.end_session_endpoint is captured from discovery, but no route or logout path reads it. OidcClient._map_claims() tolerates missing name, email, and a malformed groups claim; OidcResolver.resolve() rejects a malformed groups claim instead. The two paths therefore treat the same provider's groups claim differently.

    6. Principals and admin-provisioned passwords

    Sources: principals.py, password.py, password workflow, PostgreSQL principals, PostgreSQL credentials, memory principals, memory credentials, routes/auth/endpoints/login.py.

    • subject is globally unique across every principal; idp_subject is set only for OIDC-created users and equals subject. Both are fixed at creation. PrincipalSubjectExists is a plain Exception, not an AuthError, because it is a provisioning conflict; IdentityService and OidcAuthentication.finish translate it to the 409 UsernameTaken domain error.
    • get_user_by_subject() folds unknown username, disabled user, and service account into one None. verify_password() then runs argon2 against a dummy hash on a miss and returns False, so response time does not reveal which lookup failed. upsert_oidc_user() returns a disabled principal; the OIDC workflow is what refuses it.
    • _HASHER uses argon2 at 64 MiB, t=3, p=4. needs_rehash() lets the password workflow replace a hash made under weaker parameters after a successful verification; hashing runs in a worker thread behind a capacity limiter.
    • The Postgres credential store translates the local_credentials guard trigger into ResourceNotFound or PrincipalKindMismatch; the Postgres principal store translates a subject unique violation into PrincipalSubjectExists. The memory stores enforce the same rules by scan.

    7. Identity operations and application wiring

    Sources: identity implementation, Security ports, runtime.py, dependencies.py, routes/v1/endpoints/users.py, routes/v1/endpoints/api_keys.py, routes/v1/endpoints/service_accounts.py.

    Operation Authority check Effect
    create_user user.manage at SYSTEM Create the principal, then hash and upsert the credential with the actor's subject as updated_by. PrincipalSubjectExists becomes UsernameTaken.
    set_password user.manage at SYSTEM, target must be a user Upsert the new credential, then revoke every session and API key held by that subject.
    disable_user user.manage at SYSTEM, target must be a user Set disabled_at, then revoke every session and API key. No re-enable operation exists.
    issue_key Any authenticated actor Mint a key for the calling principal's own subject and kind; keys never escalate. The route requires an Idempotency-Key header but does not read it.
    issue_service_account_key service_account.manage at the owning organization Refuse a disabled account with Forbidden; mint with owner_kind service_account.
    disable_service_account service_account.manage at the owning organization Disable through ServiceAccounts, then revoke the account's API keys unless it was already disabled earlier.

    IdentityService is constructed per request by a dependency function. Security's authentication workflows also write these stores: pre-authentication login is a reusable operation with explicit credential checks. Routes call public operations and own transport details. ApiStores is the injection bundle a test replaces; ApiRuntime publishes the same stores plus the optional OIDC resolver and client for the lifetime of the process.

    8. Handing the principal to authorization

    Sources: access implementation, self-access operations, routes/auth/endpoints/session.py.

    Authorization reads only subject, groups, and kind. The projection drops scopes, project_id, and authentication_method before any binding is consulted, which is why an API key's restrictions never influence a decision. GET /auth/session reports the principal, its authentication method, the capabilities its bindings grant per scope, and, for a cookie session only, the CSRF token and absolute expiry. GET /auth/providers reports which login methods the deployment enables without requiring a credential.

    9. Public authentication workflows and results

    Sources: Security root exports, result values, password implementation, OIDC implementation, credential implementation, self-access implementation, trusted bootstrap.

    Password verification and optional best-effort rehash run off the event loop with a four-token limiter; rehash preserves administrative attribution. OIDC checks signed flow age, nonce, state and code, refuses disabled users and never auto-links colliding subjects. Missing provider configuration is refused at construction, before callback query validation in the API. terminate_session admits only the actor's own session; bearer logout is a no-op. The self summary returns sorted capability codes (the HTTP field still calls them effective_roles.roles). Bootstrap uses explicitly trusted deployment authority, not a scientist-supplied identity. These operations accept ports, clocks and plain values, never requests or deployment settings. The API parses the raw authorization header and retains safe redirects and cookie/CSRF policy; its OIDC factory binds validator age to the login-flow cookie's max_age. Credential resolution passes its injected clock to the key/session resolvers for post-lookup checks rather than sampling before awaits.

    10. Complete authentication error hierarchy

    Sources: authentication errors, sessions, password, principals, Security errors, Foundation base.

    Every AuthError answers 401 with its code as the problem code; the resolver's message is the only place the specific cause is stated. Revocation is checked before expiry for both keys and sessions, so a credential that is both reports revocation. PasswordRejected concerns a password being set, never one being checked. ValueError is raised by create_api_key() for an out-of-range TTL and by DevHeaderResolver for a non-development environment; both are programming or configuration errors rather than credential failures. The DomainError neighbors are declared in core/security/errors.py and carry their own status codes.

    Source and behavioral cross-checks

    The implementation snapshot was traced through constructors, fields, protocol declarations, module functions, and the request dependency. Useful behavioral entry points are:

    • Session tests, password tests, principal tests, and OIDC tests: resolver rules, dummy-digest comparison, touch throttling, hashing policy, subject uniqueness, discovery and login-flow encoding.
    • Credential dependency tests and cookie tests: branch order, CSRF enforcement, cookie attributes.
    • Login route tests, OIDC route tests, user route tests, and API key route tests: session minting, callback handling, provisioning authority, and key issuance.
    • Auth store contracts, API key conflict tests, and credential conflict tests: adapter behavior and constraint translation.

    This document describes inspected implementation; it does not claim that the application test suites were rerun to create a diagram.
